11	n=2^{s-1},\qquad j=2n-2.
12	\]
13	We will prove that \(j\) measures can always be quartered in dimension \(3n-2\), but need not be quartered in dimension \(3n-3\).

15	## 1. The upper bound
16	
17	We first recall and prove the particular product-of-spheres obstruction we need.
18	
19	### A topological lemma
20	
21	Suppose a continuous map
22	\[
23	F:S^a\times S^b\longrightarrow
24	(\mathbb R_{\alpha}\oplus\mathbb R_{\beta}
25	 \oplus\mathbb R_{\alpha\beta})^{\oplus j}
26	\]
27	is equivariant under independently changing the signs of the two sphere coordinates. Here changing the first sign acts on the three displayed coordinates as
28	\[
29	(u,v,w)\longmapsto(-u,v,-w),
30	\]
31	and changing the second acts as
32	\[
33	(u,v,w)\longmapsto(u,-v,-w).
34	\]
35	
36	If \(a+b=3j\) and
37	\[
38	[x^ay^b]\bigl(xy(x+y)\bigr)^j=1\pmod2,
39	\]
40	then \(F\) has a zero.
41	
42	**Proof.** Quotienting by the two antipodal actions, \(F\) gives a section of the vector bundle
43	\[
44	E=(\lambda_1\oplus\lambda_2\oplus
45	       (\lambda_1\otimes\lambda_2))^{\oplus j}
46	\]
47	over \(\mathbb RP^a\times\mathbb RP^b\), where \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\) are the two tautological line bundles.
48	
49	The standard mod-two cohomology calculation is
50	\[
51	H^*(\mathbb RP^a\times\mathbb RP^b;\mathbb F_2)
52	 =\mathbb F_2[x,y]/(x^{a+1},y^{b+1}),
53	\]
54	with \(w_1(\lambda_1)=x\) and \(w_1(\lambda_2)=y\). The Whitney product formula therefore gives
55	\[
56	w_{3j}(E)=\bigl(xy(x+y)\bigr)^j.
57	\]
58	Under the stated coefficient condition this class is nonzero. But a nowhere-zero section would split off a trivial line bundle, forcing the top Stiefel–Whitney class to vanish. Thus the section, and hence \(F\), has a zero. ∎
59	
60	### Applying the lemma
61	
62	Set
63	\[
64	d=3n-2.
65	\]
66	Require the first hyperplane to contain the fixed line \(\mathbb Re_1\). Its oriented defining linear forms are parametrized by
67	\[
68	S^{d-2}.
69	\]
70	All oriented affine defining forms for the second hyperplane, including the two constant forms, are parametrized by \(S^d\).
71	
72	For a defining form \(L\), write \(\sigma_L(x)=\operatorname{sgn}L(x)\). For each of the given measures \(\mu_i\), use the three test functions
73	\[
74	\int\sigma_{L_1}\,d\mu_i,\qquad
75	\int\sigma_{L_2}\,d\mu_i,\qquad
76	\int\sigma_{L_1}\sigma_{L_2}\,d\mu_i.
77	\]
78	They are continuous in the sphere parameters. Indeed, boundaries of nonconstant affine forms have measure zero, so dominated convergence applies; at a constant form the same conclusion is immediate.
79	
80	These functions have exactly the sign transformation rules in the lemma. Here
81	\[
82	a=d-2=3n-4,\qquad b=d=3n-2,\qquad a+b=3j.
83	\]
84	The relevant coefficient is
85	\[
86	[x^{3n-4}y^{3n-2}]\bigl(xy(x+y)\bigr)^{2n-2}
87	=\binom{2n-2}{n-2}.
88	\]
89	It is odd. To see this directly, since \(2n\) is a power of two, over \(\mathbb F_2\)
90	\[
91	(1+t)^{2n-2}=1+t^2+t^4+\cdots+t^{2n-2}.
92	\]
93	The exponent \(n-2\) is even and lies in this range.
94	
95	Consequently the test map has a zero. At a zero, each of the four sign regions has measure
96	\[
97	\frac14\int(1+\varepsilon_1\sigma_{L_1})
98	                 (1+\varepsilon_2\sigma_{L_2})\,d\mu_i
99	=\frac14.
100	\]
101	The second form cannot be constant. Moreover, all four sign regions are nonempty, so the hyperplanes are distinct and nonparallel. Their four sign regions are convex and are exactly the four connected components of their complement.
102	
103	Thus
104	\[
105	D_s\le 3n-2.
106	\]
107	
108	## 2. An algebraic construction for the lower bound
109	
110	We need the following explicit fact.
111	
112	### Algebraic lemma
113	
114	For every even \(n\ge4\), there exist \(2n-2\) real symmetric positive-definite \(n\times n\) matrices
115	\[
116	Q_1,\ldots,Q_{2n-2}
117	\]
118	such that
119	\[
120	a^TQ_i b=0\quad\text{for every }i
121	\]
122	is impossible when both \(a,b\in\mathbb R^n\) are nonzero.
123	
124	### Proof
125	
126	Put \(n=2k\), identifying \(\mathbb R^n\) with the complex polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\), by their coefficient vectors. Let
127	\[
128	M=2k-2,\qquad p(t)=\prod_{r=1}^{M}(t-r).
129	\]
130	
131	We will construct a symmetric real-bilinear map
132	\[
133	B:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{2n-2}
134	\]
135	with no zero on a pair of nonzero vectors, and with one coordinate equal to the ordinary inner product.
136	
137	#### Choosing a skew-symmetric matrix
138	
139	For every subset \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}\) of size \(k-1\), let
140	\[
141	f_A(t)=\prod_{r\in A}(t-r),\qquad
142	g_A(t)=\prod_{r\notin A}(t-r),
143	\]
144	and also denote their real coefficient vectors by \(f_A,g_A\).
145	
146	These vectors are linearly independent. Furthermore,
147	\[
148	C_A=f_A^Tg_A>0,
149	\]
150	because the coefficients in corresponding positions have the same alternating signs.
151	
152	We choose a real skew-symmetric matrix \(K\) such that
153	\[
154	P_A=f_A^TKg_A\ne0
155	\tag{1}
156	\]
157	for every \(A\). Here is a completely explicit choice.
158	
159	Let
160	\[
161	C_0=(M+1)^{k-1},\qquad B_0=2C_0^2,\qquad T=B_0+2.
162	\]
163	Enumerate pairs \(0\le u<v<k\) by exponents \(e=0,\ldots,h-1\), where \(h=\binom{k}{2}\), and set
164	\[
165	K_{uv}=T^e,\qquad K_{vu}=-T^e.
166	\]
167	
168	Every coefficient of \(f_A,g_A\) has absolute value at most \(C_0\). Thus
169	\[
170	f_A^TKg_A
171	=\sum_{u<v}(f_{A,u}g_{A,v}-f_{A,v}g_{A,u})T^{e(u,v)}
172	\]
173	is the evaluation at \(T\) of a nonzero integer polynomial whose coefficients have absolute value at most \(B_0\). It is nonzero because \(f_A,g_A\) are independent. Its highest nonzero term dominates all lower terms, since \(T-1>B_0\). This proves (1).
174	
175	Set
176	\[
177	S=\sum_{e=0}^{h-1}T^e,\qquad
178	\epsilon=\frac1{2(S+1)},\qquad H=I+i\epsilon K.
179	\]
180	The matrix \(H\) is Hermitian positive definite: for every \(z\in\mathbb C^k\),
181	\[
182	|z^*(iK)z|\le S\|z\|^2,
183	\]
184	and hence
185	\[
186	z^*Hz\ge(1-\epsilon S)\|z\|^2>\frac12\|z\|^2.
187	\]
188	
189	#### The bilinear map
190	
191	For complex coefficient vectors \(a,b\), take the following coordinates:
192	
193	* the real and imaginary coefficients of \(a(t)b(t)\bmod p(t)\);
194	* \(\operatorname{Re}(a^*b)\);
195	* \(\operatorname{Re}(a^*Hb)\).
196	
197	There are
198	\[
199	2(2k-2)+2=4k-2=2n-2
200	\]
201	real coordinates. Each is symmetric and bilinear over \(\mathbb R\).
202	
203	Suppose all these coordinates vanish and \(a,b\ne0\). The polynomial coordinates imply
204	\[
205	a(t)b(t)=c\,p(t),\qquad c\ne0.
206	\]
207	By unique factorization and degree counting, for some complementary factorization above,
208	\[
209	a=\alpha f_A,\qquad b=\beta g_A,
210	\qquad \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}.
211	\]
212	Write \(\gamma=\overline\alpha\beta\ne0\). The last two coordinates become
213	\[
214	C_A\operatorname{Re}\gamma,\qquad
215	\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\gamma(C_A+i\epsilon P_A)\bigr).
216	\]
217	The first vanishing forces \(\operatorname{Re}\gamma=0\). The second is then
218	\[
219	-\epsilon P_A\operatorname{Im}\gamma,
220	\]
221	which cannot vanish, since \(P_A\ne0\) and \(\gamma\ne0\). This is a contradiction.
222	
223	Finally, write these real-bilinear coordinates as \(a^TR_i b\), with symmetric real matrices \(R_i\). One of them is \(I\). Keep that matrix, and replace every other indefinite matrix \(R_i\) by
224	\[
225	R_i+L_iI
226	\]
227	for sufficiently large positive \(L_i\). All matrices are then positive definite, while their common bilinear zero set is unchanged because the coordinate \(a^Tb\) remains present. This proves the lemma. ∎
228	
229	## 3. Gaussian measures that cannot be quartered
230	
231	Return to
232	\[
233	j=2n-2,\qquad d_0=3n-3=(j-1)+n.
234	\]
235	Use coordinates
236	\[
237	(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{j-1}\times\mathbb R^n.
238	\]
239	Choose the \(j\) Gaussian measures with respective centers
240	\[
241	c_1=0,\qquad c_{r+1}=(e_r,0)\quad(1\le r\le j-1),
242	\]
243	and covariance matrices
244	\[
245	\Sigma_i=
246	\begin{pmatrix}
247	I_{j-1}&0\\
248	0&Q_i
249	\end{pmatrix},
250	\]
251	where the \(Q_i\) come from the algebraic lemma. These are nondegenerate Gaussians, so they satisfy the required absolute-continuity assumption.
252	
253	Suppose two hyperplanes quartered all these measures. Each hyperplane would individually bisect every measure.
254	
255	A hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it contains its center: its defining linear functional has a one-dimensional Gaussian distribution, whose unique median is its mean. Thus both hyperplanes contain all the \(c_i\). Their equations must therefore have the form
256	\[
257	a^Tv=0,\qquad b^Tv=0
258	\]
259	with \(a,b\ne0\).
260	
261	For the \(i\)-th Gaussian, the two defining random variables are centered jointly Gaussian with covariance
262	\[
263	a^TQ_i b.
264	\]
265	Two centered Gaussian variables have all four sign probabilities equal to \(1/4\) exactly when their covariance is zero.
266	
267	For completeness, if their correlation is strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), write
268	\[
269	Y=\rho X+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,Z
270	\]
271	using independent standard Gaussians. Conditional on \(X>0\), the probability that \(Y>0\) is strictly greater than \(1/2\). Negative correlation gives strictly less than \(1/2\), and correlations \(\pm1\) plainly do not give four quarters. Zero correlation gives independence.
272	
273	We would consequently have
274	\[
275	a^TQ_i b=0\qquad(1\le i\le j),
276	\]
277	contradicting the algebraic lemma.
278	
279	Hence the desired universal property fails in dimension \(3n-3\).
280	
281	The property is monotone in dimension: project measures onto a smaller-dimensional space, apply a partition there, and lift the hyperplanes. Absolute continuity of the projected measures follows from Fubini's theorem. Therefore failure in dimension \(3n-3\) implies
282	\[
283	D_s\ge3n-2.
284	\]
285	Together with the upper bound, this proves the formula.
286	
287	## 4. Exact Python verification
288	
289	The following code uses only exact integer and rational arithmetic. It checks:
290	
291	* the upper-bound coefficient and its parity;
292	* the explicit skew matrix and every complementary factorization;
293	* the crucial nonzero quantities \(P_A\);
294	* the bilinear matrices encoding polynomial remainders;
295	* positive definiteness of all final matrices, by strict diagonal dominance;
296	* the two-coordinate determinant certificate establishing nonsingularity.
297	
298	The proof above handles arbitrary \(s\); `check(s)` constructs and checks its finite algebraic certificate.
299	
300	```python
301	from itertools import combinations
302	from math import comb
303	import sympy as sp
304	
305	
306	def check(s):
307	    assert isinstance(s, int) and s >= 3
308	    n = 2**(s - 1)
309	    k = n // 2
310	    j = 2*n - 2
311	    d = 3*n - 2
312	
313	    # Upper-bound Euler-class coefficient.
314	    a, b = d - 2, d
315	    assert a + b == 3*j
316	    c = comb(j, a - j)
317	    assert a - j == n - 2
318	    assert c % 2 == 1
319	
320	    # Independently multiply (1+t)^j over F_2, using bits.
321	    bits = 1
322	    for _ in range(j):
323	        bits ^= bits << 1
324	    assert (bits >> (n - 2)) & 1
325	    assert bits == sum(1 << r for r in range(0, 2*n - 1, 2))
326	
327	    # Explicit lower-bound construction.
328	    t = sp.Symbol("t")
329	    M = 2*k - 2
330	    p = sp.Poly(sp.prod(t-r for r in range(1, M+1)), t)
331	
332	    Cbound = (M+1)**(k-1)
333	    Bbound = 2*Cbound**2
334	    T = Bbound + 2
335	
336	    K = sp.zeros(k)
337	    h = 0
338	    for u in range(k):
339	        for v in range(u+1, k):
340	            K[u, v], K[v, u] = T**h, -T**h
341	            h += 1
342	
343	    S = sum(T**e for e in range(h))
344	    eps = sp.Rational(1, 2*(S+1))
345	    I = sp.eye(n)
346	
347	    # Real matrix of Re(a* (I+i eps K) b).
348	    H = sp.BlockMatrix([
349	        [sp.eye(k), -eps*K],
350	        [eps*K, sp.eye(k)]
351	    ]).as_explicit()
352	
353	    assert K.T == -K
354	    assert eps*S < sp.Rational(1, 2)
355	
356	    # Real/imaginary coefficients of a(t)b(t) mod p(t).
357	    rem = [
358	        sp.rem(sp.Poly(t**r, t), p)
359	        for r in range(2*k-1)
360	    ]
361	    raw = []
362	    for ell in range(M):
363	        R = sp.Matrix(k, k, lambda u, v: rem[u+v].nth(ell))
364	        Z = sp.zeros(k)
365	        raw.append(sp.BlockMatrix([[R, Z], [Z, -R]]).as_explicit())
366	        raw.append(sp.BlockMatrix([[Z, R], [R, Z]]).as_explicit())
367	
368	    assert len(raw) + 2 == j
369	
370	    # Shift by multiples of the retained identity matrix.
371	    Q = [I, H]
372	    for R in raw:
373	        assert R.T == R
374	        L = 1 + max(
375	            sum(abs(R[u, v]) for v in range(n))
376	            for u in range(n)
377	        )
378	        Q.append(R + L*I)
379	        assert Q[-1] - L*I == R
380	
381	    # Exact positive-definiteness certificates:
382	    # symmetric, positive, strictly diagonally dominant.
383	    for A in Q:
384	        assert A.T == A
385	        assert all(
386	            A[u, u] >
387	            sum(abs(A[u, v]) for v in range(n) if v != u)
388	            for u in range(n)
389	        )
390	
391	    # Check every possible complementary factorization.
392	    count = 0
393	    roots = set(range(1, M+1))
394	    x, y = sp.symbols("x y", real=True)
395	
396	    for A in combinations(range(1, M+1), k-1):
397	        Ac = roots - set(A)
398	        f = sp.Poly(sp.prod(t-r for r in A), t)
399	        g = sp.Poly(sp.prod(t-r for r in Ac), t)
400	        assert f*g == p
401	
402	        fv = sp.Matrix([f.nth(r) for r in range(k)])
403	        gv = sp.Matrix([g.nth(r) for r in range(k)])
404	        assert max(abs(v) for v in list(fv)+list(gv)) <= Cbound
405	
406	        wedges = [
407	            fv[u]*gv[v] - fv[v]*gv[u]
408	            for u in range(k)
409	            for v in range(u+1, k)
410	        ]
411	        assert any(wedges)
412	        assert max(abs(w) for w in wedges) <= Bbound
413	
414	        P = (fv.T*K*gv)[0]
415	        assert P == sum(w*T**e for e, w in enumerate(wedges))
416	        assert P != 0
417	
418	        C = (fv.T*gv)[0]
419	        assert C > 0
420	
421	        # Embeddings alpha -> alpha*f and beta -> beta*g.
422	        Ef = sp.zeros(n, 2)
423	        Eg = sp.zeros(n, 2)
424	        for u in range(k):
425	            Ef[u, 0] = fv[u]
426	            Ef[k+u, 1] = fv[u]
427	            Eg[u, 0] = gv[u]
428	            Eg[k+u, 1] = gv[u]

430	        assert Ef.T*I*Eg == C*sp.eye(2)

432	            [C, -eps*P],
433	            [eps*P, C]
434	        ])

436	        # For alpha=(x,y), the equations in beta have determinant

441	        ])

443	            equations.det() + C*eps*P*(x*x+y*y)

106	## 2. An algebraic construction for the lower bound
107	
108	We need the following explicit fact.
109	
110	### Algebraic lemma
111	
112	For every even \(n\ge4\), there exist \(2n-2\) real symmetric positive-definite \(n\times n\) matrices
113	\[
114	Q_1,\ldots,Q_{2n-2}
115	\]
116	such that
117	\[
118	a^TQ_i b=0\quad\text{for every }i
119	\]

122	### Proof
123	
124	Put \(n=2k\), identifying \(\mathbb R^n\) with the complex polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\), by their coefficient vectors. Let
125	\[
126	M=2k-2,\qquad p(t)=\prod_{r=1}^{M}(t-r).
127	\]
128	
129	We will construct a symmetric real-bilinear map
130	\[
131	B:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{2n-2}
132	\]

134	
135	#### Choosing a skew-symmetric matrix
136	
137	For every subset \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}\) of size \(k-1\), let
138	\[
139	f_A(t)=\prod_{r\in A}(t-r),\qquad
140	g_A(t)=\prod_{r\notin A}(t-r),
141	\]
142	and also denote their real coefficient vectors by \(f_A,g_A\).
143	
144	These vectors are linearly independent. Furthermore,
145	\[
146	C_A=f_A^Tg_A>0,
147	\]
148	because the coefficients in corresponding positions have the same alternating signs.
149	
150	We choose a real skew-symmetric matrix \(K\) such that
151	\[
152	P_A=f_A^TKg_A\ne0

154	\]
155	for every \(A\). Here is a completely explicit choice.
156	
157	Let
158	\[
159	C_0=(M+1)^{k-1},\qquad B_0=2C_0^2,\qquad T=B_0+2.
160	\]

162	\[
163	K_{uv}=T^e,\qquad K_{vu}=-T^e.
164	\]
165	
166	Every coefficient of \(f_A,g_A\) has absolute value at most \(C_0\). Thus
167	\[
168	f_A^TKg_A
169	=\sum_{u<v}(f_{A,u}g_{A,v}-f_{A,v}g_{A,u})T^{e(u,v)}

171	is the evaluation at \(T\) of a nonzero integer polynomial whose coefficients have absolute value at most \(B_0\). It is nonzero because \(f_A,g_A\) are independent. Its highest nonzero term dominates all lower terms, since \(T-1>B_0\). This proves (1).

173	Set
174	\[
175	S=\sum_{e=0}^{h-1}T^e,\qquad
176	\epsilon=\frac1{2(S+1)},\qquad H=I+i\epsilon K.
177	\]
178	The matrix \(H\) is Hermitian positive definite: for every \(z\in\mathbb C^k\),
179	\[
180	|z^*(iK)z|\le S\|z\|^2,
181	\]
182	and hence
183	\[
184	z^*Hz\ge(1-\epsilon S)\|z\|^2>\frac12\|z\|^2.
185	\]

187	#### The bilinear map
188	
189	For complex coefficient vectors \(a,b\), take the following coordinates:
190	
191	* the real and imaginary coefficients of \(a(t)b(t)\bmod p(t)\);

206	\[

211	\[

224	\]

229	Return to

241	and covariance matrices

251	Suppose two hyperplanes quartered all these measures. Each hyperplane would individually bisect every measure.

253	A hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it contains its center: its defining linear functional has a one-dimensional Gaussian distribution, whose unique median is its mean. Thus both hyperplanes contain all the \(c_i\). Their equations must therefore have the form

255	a^Tv=0,\qquad b^Tv=0

257	with \(a,b\ne0\).

259	For the \(i\)-th Gaussian, the two defining random variables are centered jointly Gaussian with covariance

262	\]

272	\[
